Mac mini CI/CD build server: Xcode builds and tests on a cloud Mac

Reviewed: 2026-11-21 · WodeMac

iOS and macOS builds and tests need macOS and Xcode. On a dedicated cloud Mac you install Xcode, get xcodebuild builds and tests passing by hand, then register the Mac as a self-hosted runner for GitHub Actions or another CI platform so every push triggers a build. WodeMac's M6 Mac minis are hosted in California, online 24/7, and come with admin rights so you can set this up yourself.

Why a dedicated build Mac

A build server you control keeps the environment steady: you pin the Xcode version, simulator runtimes and dependencies, and build caches stay on disk between runs. Each WodeMac Mac mini is rented to one customer, so only your jobs run on it.

It is one option among several. Many CI platforms offer hosted macOS runners, and Apple offers its own Xcode Cloud service. Compare them on project size, control over Xcode versions and budget.

Get the build passing by hand first

Before wiring up CI, run the build in the Mac's terminal. Check the Xcode version, the project's schemes and the available simulators:

xcodebuild -version
xcodebuild -list
xcrun simctl list devices available

Then build and test (replace MyApp and the simulator name with your project and a device from the list; use -workspace for projects with an .xcworkspace):

xcodebuild -project MyApp.xcodeproj -scheme MyApp -destination "platform=iOS Simulator,name=iPhone 16" build test

Once it passes reliably by hand, hand it to CI.

Register a self-hosted runner

For GitHub Actions the general flow is below; follow the exact commands GitHub shows you and its documentation:

  1. In the repository, open Settings › Actions › Runners and choose New self-hosted runner, with macOS and ARM64.
  2. On the Mac, run the download and ./config.sh commands from that page.
  3. Run ./svc.sh install and ./svc.sh start so the runner keeps waiting for jobs as a service.
  4. In your workflow, set runs-on: [self-hosted, macOS, ARM64] and call the xcodebuild command you already tested.

GitLab Runner, Jenkins and other CI tools follow the same idea; use their own docs. GitHub recommends against using self-hosted runners with public repositories, because outside pull requests could run code on your machine.

Signing, secrets and disk space

  • Certificates and provisioning profiles come from your own Apple Developer account. Keep them in the keychain of the user the runner runs as, and test an unattended signed build once.
  • Store CI passwords and keys in your CI platform's encrypted secrets, never in the repository.
  • Create separate, least-privilege credentials for this Mac so you can revoke them on their own. WodeMac and the hosting provider keep admin access for maintenance; decide what to store with that in mind.
  • With 256GB of storage, keep only the simulator runtimes you need, clear ~/Library/Developer/Xcode/DerivedData from time to time, and remove stale simulators with xcrun simctl delete unavailable.

FAQ

Is this the same as Apple's Xcode Cloud?

No. Xcode Cloud is a CI/CD service run by Apple. WodeMac rents you a dedicated physical Mac mini, and you install Xcode and set up CI yourself. Pick whichever fits your project.

Can one Mac run several builds at once?

You can configure it, but 16GB of memory and 256GB of storage have to hold Xcode builds and simulators. Start by queueing jobs one at a time, measure, then decide whether to add Macs.

Are Xcode and the runner preinstalled?

No. The WodeMac Remote Screen app is installed at delivery; you install and update Xcode, the CI runner and other tools with your admin rights.

Can the build Mac upload to App Store Connect?

Yes, as part of your development and testing workflow, using your own Apple Developer account and certificates.
